title: Rian Johnson Says Every Film Should Still Feel Like a Risk
excerpt:
At the Marrakech Film Festival, the Knives Out filmmaker reflected on genre and creative uncertainty.
He discussed his career and resistance to simply repeating success.
body_md:
Rian Johnson reflected on his filmmaking career during an In Conversation session at the 23rd Marrakech International Film Festival. According to The Playlist, the writer-director approaches each new project with the possibility that it may not work, even after completing three Knives Out mysteries.

A lifelong admirer of Agatha Christie's fiction, Johnson described an enduring relationship with the mystery genre. The source emphasizes that he does not treat genre filmmaking as a competition to reinvent established conventions. Instead, the challenge is to find a distinctive approach within recognizable storytelling traditions.

The discussion also touched on The Brothers Bloom and the idea of avoiding the professional 'movie jail' associated with a difficult career period. The short feed excerpt does not preserve his full explanation, so the precise circumstances and quotations should not be inferred from the headline alone.

Johnson's Knives Out films have made him closely associated with contemporary ensemble mysteries. Yet the point of the Marrakech conversation is broader than any single franchise: familiarity with a successful format need not eliminate the creative uncertainty that accompanies a new film.

The report also describes a career shaped by genre interests, longtime collaborators and a desire not to repeat himself. It does not announce a new production schedule or release date in the excerpt available to this draft.

His central argument, as summarized by the source, is that taking a risk remains part of filmmaking regardless of previous success. A project should still carry the excitement and uncertainty of something that could fail.
